description: We’re a team of university students passionate about AI, technology, data, entrepreneurship, and real-world problem solving. We enjoy turning ideas into practical prototypes and competing seriously. For NASA Space Apps, we’re exploring a climate-adaptive farming solution using NASA data. We’re looking for teammates skilled in AI/ML.
summary:
Mati Kohon (Bangla for “the soil speaks”) is a crop-rotation decision-support tool for farmers in Bangladesh. NASA satellites watch these fields every day, but what they see rarely reaches the farmer. Advice arrives as a district bulletin, not for the rotation a family grows.

Mati Kohon starts from the farmer’s current rotation, sets three alternatives beside it, and replays each through 25 seasons of NASA POWER weather and GPM IMERG rain, weighted by what the farmer cares about: water, soil, income and more. For every option it explains why it was suggested, what evidence supports it, what it might gain, where data is missing, and what to check locally. SMAP, MODIS and GRACE add soil moisture, greenness and groundwater context. An agricultural officer reviews and approves each message before it reaches the farmer as a Bangla phone call (simulated in our prototype).

It matters because groundwater is falling. NASA’s groundwater data shows stored water dropping across all 64 districts, and in our Tanore pilot, Boro rice needs about four times the irrigation of lentil. One well-timed rotation choice can save water and protect the soil, and farmers deserve that evidence in their own language, before they sow.
details:
What it does

Mati Kohon helps Bangladeshi farmers and their agricultural officers compare crop rotations before the season starts. It begins with the rotation a farmer already grows, usually rice after rice. It sets three alternatives beside it and shows which option saves water, protects the soil and still fits the farming calendar, using 25 seasons of NASA Earth observations. The farmer stays in charge: the tool compares, the officer reviews, and the farmer decides.

How it works

  1. Replay the past 25 seasons. For each rotation, we run an FAO-56 water balance on NASA POWER weather and GPM IMERG rainfall for 2001–2025. Temperatures are corrected against the nearest Bangladesh Meteorological Department station, and sowing windows come from BRRI and BARI crop calendars. The replay estimates irrigation need, whether each crop fits between harvests, and heat stress at flowering and grain filling. The Tanore (Talanda union) pilot is the most detailed. Every other upazila uses its district's NASA data point.
  2. Weigh it by what the farmer values. Each option is scored on seven dimensions, including water, soil, income and pest pressure, weighted by the farmer's priorities. Scoring is rule-based and deterministic, so every number has a visible reason. Weak inputs are tagged "sample" or "assumed" on screen.
  3. Answer five questions for every option: why it was suggested, what evidence supports it, what it might gain, where data is missing, and what to check locally.
  4. Watch the season as it unfolds. A scheduled job refreshes NASA POWER conditions for all 544 upazilas every morning, adding GPM IMERG rain. SMAP soil moisture and MODIS greenness add field context. GRACE/GRACE-FO and GLDAS-2.2 show the groundwater trend behind each water-saving choice. [If built and verified: NISAR radar, checked against OPERA surface-water maps, tracks flood water draining from low river islands (chars) when monsoon cloud blocks optical satellites.]
  5. Reach the farmer through a person. The agricultural officer reads, edits and approves each message on a desk dashboard. In our prototype, the farmer then receives a Bangla voice call and can press a key to set their priority, which re-ranks the options. An Android app works offline for farmers with smartphones.

What the data showed us

  • In Tanore, one rice variety changes the whole year. BRRI dhan71 frees the field by 10 November, in time for lentil or mustard. BRRI dhan49 frees it by 19 November, which is too late.
  • Water needs differ sharply between crops. In a median winter, Boro rice needs about 797 mm of irrigation, against 199 mm for lentil, 198 for wheat and 114 for mustard.
  • Groundwater is falling. NASA groundwater data (GLDAS-2.2) shows a 147 mm drop under Tanore between 2003–07 and 2021–25. Groundwater fell in all 64 districts, significantly in 50.
  • The method holds up outside the pilot. Run with Rajshahi district's data, the replay reproduces Tanore's research figures (790 mm vs 797 mm for Boro).

Benefits and intended impact

Farmers get advice for their own rotation and priorities, not a district-wide bulletin. Officers get a queue, the reasons behind every score, and a way to record field observations that update the advice. Choosing lower-water rotations at the right time can ease pressure on falling groundwater. Adding legumes like lentil puts nitrogen back into the soil. Our next step is one season with real farmers and officers, to learn what they understand, what they trust, and what actually changes in their fields.

Tools and technologies

  • API and engine: TypeScript and Node.js, with npm workspaces for the rotation engine and the shared API types.
  • Officer dashboard: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, in Bangla and English.
  • Farmer app: Android in Kotlin with Jetpack Compose, using Room for offline storage.
  • Data research: Python scripts for acquisition and analysis, using NASA Earthdata, AppEEARS and the NASA POWER API.
  • Automation: GitHub Actions for the daily NASA update.
  • Speech: browser and Android speech recognition for Bangla voice input.
  • Phone calls: a Bangladeshi IVR provider for voice calls and keypad surveys.

What makes it creative

Most tools tell a farmer what to plant. Mati Kohon replays history: it asks how each rotation would actually have performed through 25 real seasons at that place, and shows the years it would have failed. It reaches farmers through a phone call in their own language rather than an app they may never open. It also keeps a human officer between the data and the farmer.

Factors we considered

  • Honesty about uncertainty. Where SMAP-based productivity data did not confirm the replay's dry-spell seasons at Tanore, we changed the model to count rescue irrigation as a cost. IMERG's fast-run product has read too dry since 2023, so no alert depends on a single rain source. When evidence is thin, the tool says "check the field first."
  • Resolution. NASA POWER is a coarse grid of roughly 50 km, so outside the pilot our advice is at district level, and we say so.
  • No machine-learning model. There are no labelled outcome data for rotation success here, so we kept the scoring rule-based and auditable.
  • Access. Many farmers use basic phones and have limited literacy, so voice in Bangla and officer mediation come first.
  • Gaps we state openly. Income figures are estimates until local price and cost data are added. Some heat limits are literature values, marked as assumed. Phone calls are still simulated.

    Visit our live Webapp: https://matikohon.vercel.app/
